b: There’s a house in my family—or, a house that used to be in my family. A beautiful, crumbly chateau in the south of France that my stepfather’s stepbrother had inherited from a wealthy godmother. The place was laden with debt, and expensive to run, so he had to sell it—but that’s not the point. The point is that our family, like lots of families, is complicated, with enough steps to make a ladder. Which is perhaps why I’m drawn to reading, and writing, about other complicated families in fiction—see, we’re not the only ones.

Lucky for me, stories about dysfunctional parents, children, partners, ex-partners (the list goes on) are in good supply and always have been. The Greeks were all over family drama: in Euripides’ Medea, a mother murders her children to punish her faithless husband; there’s a bucketload of domestic bloodshed in Aeschylus’s Oresteia. The Old Testament is plagued with marital woes and sibling rivalries.

If Jane Austen were here today, she might tell us that we’re drawn to families under pressure because there’s no such thing as a family that isn’t under pressure; she might even say that it’s “a truth universally acknowledged” (etc). Which, together with her writing, witty and slyly funny, is surely the secret to the enduring appeal of her classic novels. Two hundred years on, they remain a hit at the box office, with new adaptations for every generation.

In Sense and Sensibility, newly directed for the big screen by Georgia Oakley, the Dashwood sisters navigate love and loss in the face of financial ruin. Coming soon to Netflix, with a fresh script from novelist and Sunday Times columnist Dolly Alderton, Pride and Prejudice follows the Bennet sisters, who must marry well because they’re unable to inherit. So far, so old-school. But in the words of Naoise Dolan: “We would all like to be as scathing as Lizzy and to marry rich.” Where do we learn how to love and negotiate, compromise and persuade, if not from the family unit?

Joining the modern reboots of Austen is a starry revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s Tony-winning Other Desert Cities, currently showing at the Hudson Theater in New York. The play sees a daughter return to the family home in Palm Springs on Christmas Eve threatening to publish a tell-all memoir exposing an old trauma involving her brother. It’s funny and sad, a family reunion that’s as salty as it is satisfying. There’s nothing like time apart to fuel our capacity to love and wound our kin.
I didn’t set out to write a book about messy families, but I am aware that squeaky-clean ones rarely make for good (let alone convincing) reading material.

Family dramas needn’t be high drama. Just look at Tessa Hadley, who repeatedly burrows into the ordinary lives of families in her novels and short stories. Her recent foray into non-fiction, Alone with a Book: On Reading, Writing and Looking traces her development as both a reader and a writer, and explores the literary and artistic works that have kept her company along the way. There’s a brilliant essay on Elizabeth Jane Howard, best-known for the Cazalet Chronicles, a sprawling family saga packed with family get-togethers and holidays—Hadley describes them as “a true record of a real thing.” This fall, Louisa Young has picked up the thread where her aunt Elizabeth left off: The Golden Hours brings the story of the Cazalet family into the 1960s with a realistic dose of drama that’s the same, but different.

I didn’t set out to write a book about messy families, but I am aware that squeaky-clean ones rarely make for good (let alone convincing) reading material. And no wonder. What’s gripping about husbands and wives politely interacting or siblings resolving conflict without hurling abuse—or cups and saucers—across the kitchen table? Enough of the niceties! Give us tension, silence, long-suppressed secrets (simmering beneath the surface, of course)! Plus, Tolstoy was surely on to something when he wrote the famous opening line of Anna Karenina: “All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” Infinite possibilities with every fracture, twist, and tangle!

My novel, Family Friends, is set in a house similar to the one I described at the outset of this essay. It tells the story of two long-term couples and their thwarted efforts to deflect and avoid heartbreak, and unfolds during two climactic weeks, and the long, winding decades that preceded them. It’s about marriage and parenthood, the way friends and lovers change (and don’t change) over time, and families muddling through. During the writing process I was thinking about people making mistakes, and the point at which doing a bad thing makes you a bad person. Plus, what happens next? Do you carry on, because family is family, or do you reassess and walk away?

The setting may have been inspired by the beautiful, crumbly chateau in the south of France that briefly belonged to my stepfather’s stepbrother, but the seed of the book was planted several years earlier. When I was a child, we used to go on holiday with my parents’ friends and their friends’ children—big group holidays that were chaotic and loud. The parents had grown up together, and in some cases shared tangled pasts; the assumption was that us kids would rub along. We were left to our own devices in the way that children often are on holiday and would inevitably end up hearing and seeing things we shouldn’t….
Just something to bear in mind when your own family reconvenes this holiday season.
Family Friends by Chloë Ashby is available from Pegasus Books.
